idiom_name: hand-written attempt loop: classify errno, wait with nanosleep(), re-invoke
implementation_notes: C has no retry facility, so the classic structure is written out: a loop over the attempt budget, an errno or return-code classification at each call, and a wait between attempts via nanosleep() - or clock_nanosleep() with TIMER_ABSTIME when the delay must not drift - before re-invoking the operation. The one place the platform helps is signal interruption: glibc's TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY(expression) from <unistd.h> re-evaluates a call that failed with EINTR, which restarts a syscall rather than implementing a transient-fault policy, and it must not be mistaken for the pattern because EINTR says nothing about whether the operation will succeed later. nanosleep() itself reports EINTR with the remaining time in rem, so the delay must be resumed or recomputed; treat a fixed maximum attempt count plus an absolute deadline as the loop invariant.
pitfalls: TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY only covers EINTR: wrapping a call in it looks like retry but never repeats a refused connection, a timeout or a 503.
nanosleep() returns early on a signal with the remaining time in rem; discarding rem shortens every delay when the process receives signals.
errno is only meaningful immediately after the failing call and is clobbered by any other library call - classify and copy it before logging or sleeping.
Retrying a non-idempotent write (a POST, a partially completed write() loop) after a timeout can duplicate the effect, so the operation must be repeat-safe first.
